blocks.text: A conveyor drive motor runs at 3900 rpm with no load, then slows only slightly when a heavy crate lands on the belt, yet its supply current jumps several-fold. The permanent-magnet DC motor is the workhorse actuator of mechatronics because torque, current and speed are tied together by just two numbers.

blocks.markdown: A **permanent-magnet DC motor** has a rotor (armature) winding of resistance $R_a$ carrying current $I_a$ in a fixed magnetic field. The field acts on the current to produce **torque**, and the winding moving through the field generates a voltage opposing the supply, the **back-EMF**. In SI units both effects are described by the same constant $K$.

blocks.title: Motor constants
blocks.text: Torque is proportional to armature current: $T=K_t I_a$ (N m, with $K_t$ in N m/A). Back-EMF is proportional to angular speed: $E_b=K_e\omega$ (V, with $K_e$ in V s/rad and $\omega$ in rad/s). In consistent SI units $K_t=K_e=K$.

blocks.caption: Torque, back-EMF and the armature voltage equation (steady state, armature inductance neglected)

blocks.markdown: Think of the back-EMF as the motor's own speed sensor fighting the supply. At standstill $E_b=0$ and the full voltage drives current through only $R_a$ (a large **stall current** $V_a/R_a$). As the motor accelerates, $E_b$ grows, the net voltage $V_a-E_b$ falls, and so does current and torque. The motor stops accelerating when its torque equals the load torque: the **steady state**.

blocks.caption: Steady-state current and speed for a given load torque; the speed-torque line falls linearly with load

blocks.title: Steady-state operating point
blocks.prompt: A motor has $K=0.050$ N m/A, $R_a=1.2\ \Omega$ and is supplied with 24 V. The load torque is 0.15 N m. Find the armature current, back-EMF and speed in rad/s and rpm.

steps.text: Speed from the back-EMF constant, then convert to rpm.

blocks.answer: I_a = 3.0 A, E_b = 20.4 V, speed = 408 rad/s (about 3900 rpm).

blocks.title: No-load speed and stall
blocks.prompt: For the same motor and 24 V supply find the ideal no-load speed and the stall torque.

steps.text: Stall: $\omega=0$ so $E_b=0$ and only $R_a$ limits current.

blocks.answer: No-load speed 480 rad/s (4584 rpm); stall current 20 A giving stall torque 1.0 N m. Operating at 3.0 A, the motor is far from stall.

blocks.markdown: **Controlling speed with PWM.** To run a motor slower, we must lower the average voltage. Dropping voltage in a series resistor wastes power as heat. A better method is **pulse-width modulation**: a transistor switches the full supply $V_s$ on and off rapidly with duty cycle $D$. The winding inductance and rotor inertia filter the pulses, so the motor sees an average $V_{avg}=D\,V_s$. Steady-state speed follows the earlier equations with $V_a$ replaced by $D V_s$, so speed is nearly proportional to duty cycle at light load.

items: Higher duty cycle: higher average voltage, higher no-load speed.
Greater load torque: higher current, lower speed (more resistive drop).
The transistor is either fully on or off, so it dissipates little power.
Reversing the supply polarity reverses the direction of rotation.

blocks.title: Respect the stall current
blocks.text: At start-up, $E_b=0$ and the current is $V_a/R_a$, often ten or more times the rated value. Limit it with PWM ramp-up or current limiting to protect the driver and windings.

points: $T=K I_a$ and $E_b=K\omega$ with the same constant $K$ in SI units; $V_a=I_aR_a+E_b$.
At steady state torque balances load: $I_a=T_{load}/K$ and $\omega=(V_a-I_aR_a)/K$.
PWM sets average motor voltage $V_{avg}=D V_s$ efficiently, so duty cycle controls speed.

questions.stem: A motor with torque constant $K_t=0.080$ N m/A carries an armature current of 5.0 A. What torque does it produce?

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this divides K by I.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this divides I by K, giving the units of A/(N m/A).
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this multiplies by 50, a misplaced decimal.

questions.explanation: Torque is directly proportional to armature current, $T=K_tI_a=0.080\times5.0=0.40$ N m. The constant has units of N m per ampere, so multiplication gives N m.

questions.stem: As a DC motor accelerates at constant supply voltage, what happens to its armature current?

options.text: It falls, because back-EMF grows and reduces the net voltage across R_a

questions.correctOptionText: It falls, because back-EMF grows and reduces the net voltage across R_a

distractorRationale.a: Correct: I_a = (V_a - E_b)/R_a falls as E_b rises.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: current is driven by V_a - E_b, which shrinks.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: V_a/R_a is the stall current at zero speed only.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: current is zero only when E_b = V_a at the no-load limit.

questions.explanation: The armature equation gives $I_a=(V_a-E_b)/R_a$ and $E_b=K\omega$ grows with speed. So the current is largest at start-up and falls as the motor speeds up.

questions.stem: At a fixed supply voltage, the load torque on a DC motor is increased. In the new steady state the motor has:

options.text: Lower speed and higher armature current
Higher speed and higher armature current
Lower speed and lower armature current

questions.correctOptionText: Lower speed and higher armature current

distractorRationale.a: Correct: higher torque needs higher I_a, whose R_a drop lowers E_b and hence speed.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: speed cannot rise because the I_a R_a drop grows.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: current must rise to supply the extra torque.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: torque balance forces the current to change.

questions.explanation: Steady state needs $K I_a=T_{load}$, so more load means more current. A larger $I_aR_a$ drop leaves less for $E_b=K\omega$, so the speed falls slightly.

questions.stem: A motor on a 48 V bus must see an average of 30 V from a PWM driver. What duty cycle is required?

distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this inverts the ratio, 48/30, giving more than 100 %.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this equates duty with the voltage value.

questions.explanation: Average voltage is $D\,V_s$, so $D=30/48=0.625$ or 62.5 %. The inverted ratio would exceed 100 %, which is impossible.

questions.stem: A motor with $K=0.030$ V s/rad is on a 12 V supply with negligible friction and no load. What is the ideal no-load speed?

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this multiplies K by V.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this halves the voltage, which is not required.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: 3820 is the rpm value; the question asks for rad/s and this mixes units.

questions.explanation: With no load $I_a=0$, so $E_b=V_a$ and $\omega_0=V_a/K=12/0.030=400$ rad/s. That is about 3820 rpm, which is a common unit-confusion distractor.

questions.stem: A motor with $K=0.080$ N m/A (V s/rad) and $R_a=0.80\ \Omega$ is supplied with 12 V and drives a load torque of 0.20 N m. Find the steady-state speed in rad/s.
questions.explanation: Current $I_a=0.20/0.080=2.5$ A. Back-EMF $E_b=12-2.5\times0.80=10$ V. Speed $\omega=E_b/K=10/0.080=125$ rad/s.

questions.stem: A motor with back-EMF constant 0.080 V s/rad is turned at 3000 rpm by an external drive with its terminals open. What voltage (in V) appears across the terminals?
questions.explanation: Convert $3000$ rpm to $\omega=3000\times2\pi/60=314.2$ rad/s. Then $E_b=K\omega=0.080\times314.2=25.1$ V. This is the generator effect and is the basis of the tachometer.

questions.stem: A motor with $K=0.10$ N m/A and $R_a=1.0\ \Omega$ is driven from a 24 V supply by a PWM stage at 70 % duty cycle (average voltage applied, inductance smooths the current). The load torque is 0.60 N m. Find the steady-state speed in rad/s.
questions.explanation: Average voltage is $0.70\times24=16.8$ V. Current is $0.60/0.10=6.0$ A, so $E_b=16.8-6.0\times1.0=10.8$ V. Speed is $10.8/0.10=108$ rad/s.

questions.stem: Show that the torque constant and the back-EMF constant of an ideal DC motor are numerically equal in SI units, using conservation of energy.
markingGuide: Electrical power converted to mechanical is E_b I_a
Mechanical power output is T omega
Substitutes T = K_t I_a and E_b = K_e omega to get K_e omega I_a = K_t I_a omega
Concludes K_e = K_t (losses in R_a, friction are separate)
questions.explanation: The power crossing from electrical to mechanical form is $E_bI_a$, and the mechanical power is $T\omega$. For a lossless conversion these are equal: $K_e\omega I_a=K_tI_a\omega$, so $K_e=K_t$ in SI units. Winding loss $I_a^2R_a$ is separate and does not affect this equality.

questions.stem: Explain how varying the PWM duty cycle controls the speed of a DC motor, and why this is more efficient than dropping the voltage across a series resistor.
markingGuide: States average voltage is D times supply voltage
Explains winding inductance and rotor inertia smooth the pulses so the motor responds to the average
Links lower average voltage to lower no-load speed omega = V_avg/K and speed under load
Explains the switch is fully on or fully off so it dissipates little power
Explains a series resistor dissipates I^2 R as heat and so wastes energy
questions.explanation: The driver switches the supply on for a fraction $D$ of each period, so the motor responds to $V_{avg}=D\,V_s$ and its speed follows $\omega=(V_{avg}-I_aR_a)/K$. Because the transistor is either on (small voltage drop) or off (zero current), little power is lost in it. A series resistor carrying motor current $I$ would dissipate $I^2R$ as heat.
